questions.prompt: When does the lifetime of an object with a non-trivial destructor end according to [basic.life]?
options: Only after free() or operator delete returns the storage to the OS
Once all pointers to the object go out of scope
The moment the destructor call starts, before its body finishes
When the last statement inside the destructor body finishes executing
questions.explanation: Under [basic.life]/1, for an object of a class type with a non-trivial destructor, lifetime ends when the destructor call starts (or when storage is reused/released without running the destructor).

questions.prompt: Which C++23 standard library function starts the lifetime of an implicit-lifetime type T in existing raw bytes without copying or overwriting their contents?
options: std::start_lifetime_as<T>
std::launder<T>
std::construct_at<T>
std::assume_aligned<T>
questions.explanation: C++23 std::start_lifetime_as<T>(ptr) implicitly creates an object of implicit-lifetime type T whose value corresponds to the existing byte representation at ptr, avoiding a redundant std::memcpy.

questions.prompt: In C++17 and C++20 (before C++23 P2718R0), what happens in this range-based for loop?
options: Well-defined because range-for always extends the entire initializer expression
Ill-formed because make_holder() returns a prvalue
Well-defined only if int x is replaced with auto&& x
Undefined behavior because the Holder temporary is destroyed before the loop body begins
questions.explanation: Before C++23, range-for desugared to auto&& __range = make_holder().items;. Because __range bound to the member reference returned/accessed rather than extending Holder across the whole expression, Holder died at the semicolon before iteration started. C++23 P2718R0 fixed this specifically for range-for.

questions.prompt: Why does std::string_view sv = std::string("hello") + " world"; produce a dangling view despite const reference extension rules?
options: std::string_view allocates on the heap and leaks
Temporary lifetime extension applies to direct reference bindings, not user-defined class values like std::string_view
std::string literals are destroyed at block entry
String concatenation yields an lvalue rather than a prvalue
questions.explanation: Lifetime extension under [class.temporary] extends a temporary ONLY when bound directly to a reference (const T& or T&&). std::string_view is a class type holding a pointer and length; the temporary std::string dies at the semicolon, leaving sv dangling.

questions.prompt: After destroying a Node with a const int member and constructing a new Node in the same storage via ::new (p) Node{2}, why is reading p->id directly undefined behavior?
options: Because Node has a const non-static data member, old pointer p is not transparently replaceable under [basic.life]/8
Because placement new changes the virtual address of p
Because const int members cannot be destroyed explicitly
Because Node lacks a user-declared move constructor
questions.explanation: Under [basic.life]/8, an old pointer automatically refers to a newly created object at the same storage ONLY if the class has no const or reference non-static data members (among other rules). You must use the pointer returned by placement new or std::launder(p).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true of std::launder(p) when p points to raw bytes where no object of type T has ever been constructed?
options: std::launder(p) implicitly begins the lifetime of a T at p
std::launder(p) disables strict aliasing rules for T
Calling std::launder(p) violates its precondition because no live object of type T exists at that address
std::launder(p) converts any void* into a valid T* safely
questions.explanation: Per [ptr.launder], std::launder(p) requires that an object of type T is ALREADY within its lifetime at the address represented by p. It never creates an object (use placement new, std::construct_at, or std::start_lifetime_as for that).
